## SCORE in brief {#score-in-brief .smaller}

::: {.fs-80}
| Repetition | The study | What came back |
|:-----|:-----|:-----|
| **Reproduction** – same data, same analysis | 600 papers from 62 journals, 2009–2018 [@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial] | Of the 143 that could be assessed, **53.6%** reproduced precisely and **73.5%** at least approximately; counting the papers that nobody could check, about **18%** |
| **Robustness** – same data, other analyses | Multi100: 100 studies, at least 5 analysts each [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness] | **74%** of reanalyses reached the same conclusion; **34%** came within ±0.05 *d* of the original effect size |
| **Replication** – new data | 274 claims, independent data [@TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial] | **55.1%** significant again; the median effect size fell from *r* = 0.25 to 0.10 |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Measured on the same body of papers, the three are **essentially uncorrelated**: knowing how a finding fared on one tells you almost nothing about the others.
:::

::: notes
SCORE, a programme funded by the research agency of the US Department of Defense, took a sample of social-science papers and put their central claims through each of the three repetitions on the grid. Reproduction first: of six hundred papers, the authors supplied data for about a quarter, and of the hundred and forty-three that could be assessed, about half reproduced precisely and three quarters approximately. Count the papers that nobody could check, and the rate is about eighteen per cent. Robustness was Multi100, where at least five analysts reanalysed each claim: three quarters reached the same conclusion, but only a third came close to the original effect size. Replication on new data: fifty-five per cent significant again, with effect sizes more than halved. [advance] And the three barely predict one another, so for any one paper you have to ask which of the three it passed.
:::

## What a Multi100 analyst received {#inside-multi100-what-an-analyst-was-sent .smaller}

::: {.small}
- A **published paper**, in full and not blinded, so the original estimates were in view
- Its **central claim**, in one sentence, usually taken from the abstract
- The **data**, or directions for fetching them
- No instructions on method – any analysis you can defend
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
And two things that no analyst was told: **who the other analysts were**, and **what they were finding**.
:::

::: {.src}
@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness. Registered protocol: osf.io/dy68c
:::

::: notes
Multi100 handed a hundred published studies to at least five independent analysts each, and I was one of those analysts, on a different paper from the one we work on today. Let me describe what that was like from the inside, because it shapes how you read the results. What arrived was the published paper, the whole thing and not blinded, so the original estimates were in view, and if anything that pulls you towards the original answer. With it came the central claim of the paper in a single sentence, usually taken from the abstract, and the data or directions for fetching them. What did not arrive was any instruction on method: analyse it however you can defend. And two things stayed hidden throughout, who the other analysts were and what any of them were finding. The isolation was part of the design, because it is what makes the spread at the end mean something.
:::

## The two Multi100 tasks {#two-tasks-months-apart .smaller}

::: {.small}
**Task 1 – free reanalysis.** Reanalyse the claim however you see fit, then record one conclusion: evidence for the claim, evidence for the opposite, no evidence either way, or evidence for the null hypothesis.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
**Task 2 – constrained reanalysis.** Once Task 1 was in, instructions arrived: report a single main result from the family of *z*, *t*, *F* or $\chi^2$ tests (or an alternative or non-parametric version), with an instruction for each claim that fixed one or two details of the analysis.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Task 1 measures whether analysts reach the same verdict. Task 2 makes their *numbers* comparable, since five answers to five different questions cannot be averaged.
:::

::: notes
The study ran in two stages, and the distinction matters for everything that follows. Task one was complete freedom: reanalyse the claim however you see fit, and record one categorical conclusion out of four, evidence for the claim, evidence for the opposite, no evidence either way, or evidence for the null hypothesis. [advance] Once that was submitted, task two arrived. It asked for a single main result in the form of a test statistic, and it came with a short instruction for each claim that pinned down one or two details of the analysis. [advance] The order matters because the two tasks measure different things. Task one asks whether independent analysts reach the same verdict. Task two asks whether they produce the same number, and that question can only be asked once everyone is answering roughly the same question, which is what the instructions were for. We will read the instruction for our own claim later.
:::

## Results on a common scale {#how-a-hundred-studies-become-one-number .smaller}

::: {.small}
- Every analyst reports a test statistic in whatever form the model produces – **t**, **z**, **F**, $\chi^2$ – with its degrees of freedom or its sample size
- Each is converted to a **partial correlation** *r* and a standardised **Cohen's *d***, so that a regression fitted in Stata and a test computed in R can be read on one axis
- A **peer panel** judges whether each pipeline is an appropriate analysis of the claim
- Only then can you ask how far apart several defensible answers are
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Standardising makes the comparison possible, but it assumes that the analysts are estimating **the same quantity**, and that the numbers fed into each conversion count the units that carry the evidence. Hold both thoughts.
:::

::: notes
Even with the question pinned down, the answers arrive in different forms. Everyone reports the test statistic that their model happens to produce, a t, a z, an F or a chi-square, with its degrees of freedom or its sample size. Multi100 converted those onto a common scale, a partial correlation and a standardised difference, so that a regression fitted in Stata and a test computed in R could be placed on the same axis. Alongside that, a peer panel judged whether each pipeline was an appropriate analysis of the claim at all, so the spread that comes out of the study is a spread among analyses that passed review. [advance] Putting several numbers on one axis takes two things for granted. One is that they estimate the same quantity, and a good deal of what follows is about what happens when they do not. The other is that each conversion counts the units that actually carry the evidence.
:::

## The question of the paper {#the-question-of-the-paper .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **The question.** Do the officials who control access to a public programme answer people differently by race or ethnicity? Officials who deal with the public directly, and decide how much help to give, are **street-level bureaucrats** [@Lipsky1980StreetLevelBureaucracy]
- **The method.** An **audit study** sends matched requests, or matched applicants, that differ in one characteristic, and compares what comes back [@BertrandMullainathan2004AreEmilyGreg; @Pager2003MarkCriminalRecord]. Here the characteristic is a name
- **What it added.** Audits of politicians and local election officials had found discrimination [@ButlerBroockman2011PoliticiansRaciallyDiscriminate; @WhiteEtAl2015WhatNeedVote]. This one asks about a bureaucracy that hands out a valuable benefit and is less tied to politics
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The paper is an experiment published in 2017 [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect]. From here on I call its two authors **the original authors (OAs)**.
:::

::: notes
The case of the day is a paper in the American Journal of Political Science, and I will call its two authors the original authors, or OAs, from here on, because the course is about the claim and its analyses rather than about the people who made it. The question is old and important: do the officials who stand between citizens and a public programme answer people differently by race or ethnicity? Sociologists call those officials street-level bureaucrats, after Lipsky, because they deal with the public directly and have discretion over how much help to give. The method is the audit study, which sends matched requests that differ in one characteristic and compares the responses. Earlier audits had found discrimination by politicians and election officials. The OAs asked whether the same holds in a bureaucracy that hands out something valuable, access to public housing, and is further from politics.
:::

## The email {#the-email}

::: {.claimcard .fs-80}
Hello,

My name is X and I'm trying to figure out how to apply for public housing. I believe I may be eligible.

Can you direct me to information about applying for public housing here? I also heard there might be a wait list for this program. How long is it?

Thanks, X
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Four outcomes were coded from what came back: any reply, a reply within 24 hours, information about the wait list, and the tone – "whether the emailer is addressed by proper name. We were lenient in coding 'yes.' A named salutation could be as causal [sic] as 'Hi Brett' or as formal as 'Dear Ms. Martinez.'"
:::

::: {.src}
@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect, accepted manuscript, pp. 10 and 12–14.
:::

::: notes
This is the whole email, word for word, with X standing for the name of the sender. It is short, polite and plausible: someone who thinks they may be eligible asks how to apply and how long the wait list is. Every authority received exactly this text, and the only thing that differed was the name at the top and at the bottom. [advance] From what came back the OAs coded four outcomes. Did the authority reply at all, did it reply within a day, did it give information about the wait list, and what was the tone. Tone was measured in one way: whether the reply addressed the sender by name. The coding was lenient, so "Hi Brett" counts and so does "Dear Ms. Martinez". The claim that we work on today is about that last outcome.
:::

Above, the official, drawn pale because nobody observed them: workload, habits of courtesy, attitudes, anything about the person who reads the email, which affects both whether they reply and how they open. ::: {.fragment .small}
Conditioning on a variable that the treatment can change is **post-treatment conditioning**: the gap among replies mixes an effect on **how** officials write with a difference in **which** officials wrote [@MontgomeryEtAl2018HowConditioningPosttreatment; @Coppock2019AvoidingPosttreatmentBias].

::: notes
Now draw a box around the reply, because that is what the paper does when it compares greetings among replies only. The reply is caused by the name, and also by the official, so it is a common effect of the two, a collider. Conditioning on a collider opens a path between its causes: among the replies, the name and the official are no longer independent. If a Hispanic name discourages some officials from replying, the officials who answered Santiago are a different mix from those who answered Brett, perhaps the more conscientious ones, perhaps the busier ones. Their habits of greeting then travel along the red path into the comparison. [advance] The general name for this is post-treatment conditioning, conditioning on something that the treatment can change, and it can produce a gap even where the name has no effect on tone at all. Coppock wrote about it for exactly this kind of audit experiment.
:::

## Counting every delivered email {#counting-every-delivered-email .smaller}

::: {.small}
- Count **every delivered email**, with no reply counted as no greeting: no box, nothing opened, and the groups stay as randomisation made them
- The outcome changes with it: a **reply that greets the sender by name**, which combines whether a reply came with how it began
:::

::: {.small}
| Emails counted | Hispanic names | White names | Difference |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Coded replies (n = 362) | 41.2% | 61.1% | −19.97 points |
| Delivered emails (n = 662) | 21.6% | 35.0% | −13.34 points |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Two defensible questions. Among the replies: the question of the claim, about tone, but an effect of the name alone only if the name did not change who replied. Among all emails: an effect of the name that randomisation protects, on a different outcome. The reply gap of −4.8 points (p = 0.214) makes a large selection unlikely, without ruling it out.
:::

::: notes
The remedy is to remove the box. Count every email that arrived, and treat an email that drew no reply as one that drew no greeting. Now nothing is conditioned on, and the groups are exactly as the random number generator made them. But the outcome has changed with the denominator: it is now a reply that greets the sender by name, which combines whether a reply came with how it began. Among replies, forty-one per cent against sixty-one, a gap of twenty points. Among all delivered emails, twenty-two against thirty-five, a gap of thirteen. [advance] Neither is wrong. The comparison among replies answers the question of the claim, about tone, and is clean only if the name did not change who replied. The comparison among all emails is clean by design, and answers a related but different question. One of the five analysts made exactly this move.
:::

- **Specification curve analysis** [@SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis] – the same move for *model* choices, plus a visual grammar: estimates on top, the choices that produced each one underneath

::: notes
A brief history, because the vocabulary is a mess and knowing which word came from where helps. Multiverse analysis is Steegen and colleagues in 2016, and it grew out of data-processing choices specifically – how you code a variable, which cases you exclude, how you combine items – with the proposal that you report the whole set of datasets that your choices could have produced. Specification curve analysis is Simonsohn, Simmons and Nelson, making the same move for model choices and adding a visual grammar: estimates plotted on top, and underneath them a panel showing which choices produced each one. The vibration of effects is the same idea arrived at independently in epidemiology, which suggests that it is a natural response to the problem. And there is now a book-length treatment with computational recipes. Under different names, they all make the same proposal: stop treating your analytical choices as invisible, and enumerate them.
:::

| | The original audit | The replication |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Authorities | those matched with a core city: 1,017 | the authorities on the HUD list: 3,050 |

::: notes
Set the two studies side by side and the differences are worth reading row by row, because each is a candidate explanation. The replication emailed the authorities on the HUD list, not only those near a core city, so its population of officials is larger and more varied. It randomised within states. Its names were different, all male, and pre-tested to vary ethnicity without varying class. It coded a friendly reply as any use of a name, which is close to the lenient coding of the original but not identical. Its census covariates come from a later year. And it is later in time. None of these differences is a flaw: a replication is supposed to take the question to new data. But the list is also the list of reasons why the two results might differ without either study being wrong.
:::

The original comparison detects a gap of 20 points almost always (0.97), but one of 10 points less than half the time (0.48). The replication has 0.78 for 10 points.

::: notes
One more lens: power, the probability that a study of a given size detects a gap of a given size. At a white share of sixty-one per cent, the original comparison, with about a hundred and eighty replies a group, detects a twenty-point gap almost every time. But its power for a ten-point gap is under one half, and for thirteen points about seven in ten. The replication, with three hundred and sixty-nine replies a group, has nearly eight in ten for ten points. Two consequences. A replication of this size would have found a gap of ten points about four times in five, and a larger one more often still, had there been one. And when a study with modest power for realistic effects does reach significance, its estimate tends to overstate the true effect, because only the lucky draws clear the bar. The published interval runs from minus thirty to minus ten.
:::

::: notes
This is the lesson of the case, and of the course. On the original data the claim is hard to dislodge: every justifiable analysis finds the gap, and only its size moves. [advance] But every one of those analyses works on the same thousand emails, the same six names, the same officials in the same week of 2014. A specification curve varies the analysis and holds the sample fixed, so it cannot tell you what a new sample would show. [advance] Robustness to analytic choices on one sample is a different property from replicability. [advance] Why might the two studies differ? The names are one candidate: names that are meant to indicate one group are not all read the same way, and Santiago and Gabriela may also have read as younger. Chance is another, given the power of the original design. And time and place are a third. The replication does not tell us which.
:::

## Two points from the literature {#two-sentences-worth-keeping}

::: {.claimcard}
"the common single-path analyses in social and behavioural research should not be simply assumed to be robust to alternative analyses" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]
:::

::: {.claimcard}
A blueprint: precise question → causal reasoning (DAG) → multiverse → sensitivity analysis [@AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial]
:::

::: {.small}
- Same-conclusion robustness and same-*number* robustness are different bars
- Justifiability is the criterion – choose with reasons, show the spread
:::

::: notes
The first point comes from the Multi100 paper: single-path analyses should not simply be assumed robust. A single path can be a good path, and still the reader is owed the space around it, so a report needs the chosen path and the alternatives together. From Auspurg and Brüderl comes the constructive recipe that we followed today: a precise question, explicit assumptions drawn as a graph, a multiverse, and a sensitivity analysis. And keep the two robustness standards apart in your own writing: the same conclusion, which was reached by seventy-four per cent of the reanalyses in Multi100, and the same number, which only thirty-four per cent came close to. When you claim robustness, say which one you mean.
:::
